facts.claim: "How to Love" is track 5 of 8 on Buffalo Nichols' self-titled debut album, released 15 October 2021 on Fat Possum Records.
Fat Possum describes the album as its first solo blues signing in nearly 20 years.
The label's album notes say the record deals with empathy and forgiveness on "How to Love," which they call a poignant, ever-building melody.

Uncut reads the song as Nichols counting the lessons and scars from a relationship, knowing his lover took just as many. The refrain is that the way they hurt you showed you how to love, and the way you hurt me showed me how to love.
The album is composed largely of demos and studio sessions recorded between Wisconsin and Texas.
Nichols recorded demos for many of the album's songs in Milwaukee. He also recorded at Electric Deluxe, the South Austin home studio of Black Pumas' Adrian Quesada.
The album also had additional sessions at Sonic Ranch in Tornillo, Texas.

Austin drummer Brannen Temple plays on a couple of songs on the album. Discogs credits Temple (drums), Matthew Wilson (bass, drums), Jess McIntosh (violin), Danny Zelonky (recorded by) and Clay Jones (mixed and mastered by) on the album.

Nichols told an interviewer that before writing one song he had written many political songs that demand something of the audience, and that people then wanted to discuss those songs after shows. He said he tries to put the idea into the music so nobody has to tell him what they think afterward. The interview discusses "How to Love" and "Back On Top" as love songs.

Nichols was born Carl Nichols in Houston, Texas, and raised in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. He first played in the duo Nickel & Rose with Johanna Rose before going solo as Buffalo Nichols, and he later based himself in Austin.

research.lineage: The song sits in contemporary folk-blues, with fingerstyle and slide guitar influenced by Bentonia, Mississippi players such as Skip James, and with Nichols stating an aim to put more Black stories into folk and blues.

draft:
The last choruses of **How to Love** change a few small words and turn the whole song inside out. For most of its length Buffalo Nichols sings a wounded thank-you note, "the way you hurt me showed me how to love," the kind of thing people tell themselves to make a breakup worth something. Then, in the final verse, years have passed. He barely recognizes the person who walked out the door, decides they couldn't hurt a fly, and the refrain swings around to face them: "the way they hurt you showed you." The hurt stops belonging to him alone. It becomes a chain, handed down from whoever got to his ex first.

That turn lands because the song lets him be a mess before he earns it. The opening blames a pretty girl for every ugly thing he did, the cigarettes and the diamond rings, half joke and half alibi. He insists he isn't heartless, then admits there's a lot he hardly understands. He sold everything for a lie, and the second verse ends on the bitterest image in the song: love could have been the cure, "but your love was a disease." Gratitude and self-pity share the same chorus and never settle. Even the first refrain carries a sting he leaves alone, sitting right after the admission that in the end he wasn't good enough.

The playing keeps all of that low to the ground. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar carries the song, a slide catching some of the notes, over a walking bass and light drums: brushes on the snare, a soft kick. The tempo is slow and the shuffle relaxed, never pushed. A clean electric guitar traces a simple melody against the vocal. Nichols sings in a slightly raspy, conversational voice with no harmonies to cushion it, telling the story more than performing it. The room sounds warm and natural, finished without being buffed to a shine.

The guitar style has roots in the Bentonia, Mississippi players like Skip James. Nichols has said he wants to put more Black stories into folk and blues, and Fat Possum signed him as its first solo blues act in nearly 20 years. Here he bends that tradition toward a love song about forgiveness. He has also talked about moving away from political songs that demand something of an audience. He'd rather build the idea into the music, so nobody has to explain it to him after the show. In this song the idea is empathy, and he never says the word. He just changes who's getting hurt.

It sticks because it walks you from blaming someone to understanding them inside a single refrain, then leaves you wondering who taught you to love the way you do.
